results.answer:
The main findings of the Library of Things pilot evaluation were:

- **Reach and growth:** By March 2025, **1,936 people** had registered as borrowers across the three branches. Loans increased from **2,214** in year one to **3,498** in year two, a rise of **58 percent**.
- **Repeat use:** Of the **1,421** borrowers who made at least one loan, **668** borrowed more than once, a **repeat borrowing rate of 47 percent**.
- **Who it reached:** Of the **1,490** borrowers with a usable home postcode, **611 (41 percent)** lived in neighbourhoods in the two most deprived quintiles, which was close to the town’s **40 percent** share.
- **Household savings:** Survey respondents reported a median saving of **GBP 85** over the previous twelve months; for decorating equipment, the median was **GBP 120**.
- **Avoided purchases and emissions:** The pilot is estimated to have avoided the purchase of about **1,130 items**, corresponding to around **38 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent** over the two years.
- **Condition of items:** Damage was recorded on **3.1 percent of loans**; **19 items** were lost or never returned, equal to **0.3 percent of loans**. Repairs and replacements cost **GBP 2,460** in total.
- **Overall conclusion:** The report says the pilot **met its aims for reach and regular use**, delivered savings and environmental benefits, and recommends that the scheme **continues**, with changes to damage recording and item selection.

ANSWER: The pilot reached 1,936 registered borrowers, loans grew by 58 percent year-on-year, repeat borrowing was 47 percent, registrations from deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with the town’s population share, borrowers reported a median saving of GBP 85, the pilot avoided about 1,130 purchases and around 38 tonnes of CO2e, and most items came back in good condition with damage recorded on 3.1 percent of loans.

     1	Borrowing instead of buying: evaluation of the Brackenford Library of Things pilot, April 2023 to March 2025
     2	Northfold Social Research, for Brackenford Libraries. Final report, September 2025.
     3	Abstract
     4	The Brackenford Library of Things lends household tools and equipment from three branch
     5	libraries for a small fee. This report evaluates the first two years of the pilot, from
     6	April 2023 to March 2025, using membership and loan records, a survey of borrowers and the
     7	checks that staff make when items are returned. Almost 2,000 residents registered as
     8	borrowers, and loans grew by 64 percent between the first and second years. Borrowers
     9	reported modest savings, and most items came back in good condition. Registrations from
    10	deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with their share of the town's population. We
    11	recommend that the scheme continues, with changes to how damage is recorded and how new
    12	items are chosen.
    13	1 Introduction
    14	Libraries of things apply the familiar library model to objects that households need only
    15	occasionally, such as drills, gazebos and sewing machines. Their supporters argue that
    16	borrowing saves money, reduces the number of rarely used items that people buy, and brings
    17	people into libraries who would not otherwise visit.
    18	Brackenford Libraries opened its Library of Things in April 2023 with a grant of GBP 96,000
    19	from the Halden Foundation, which also funded this evaluation. The pilot ran from three of
    20	the town's seven branch libraries: Central, Eastgate and Millbrook.
    21	
    22	Items could be reserved online and collected from any of the three branches, and loans
    23	lasted up to seven days. This report sets out what the pilot achieved against the aims
    24	agreed with the funder: to reach a broad range of residents, to build regular use, to save
    25	households money and to reduce waste. Section 2 summarises earlier evaluations of similar
    26	schemes, Section 3 describes our methods, Section 4 presents the results, and Sections 5 to
    27	7 discuss them.
    28	2 Previous studies
    29	Published evaluations of libraries of things are few, and most describe a single scheme in
    30	its first years. A survey of 14 schemes in England found a median of 1,150 registered
    31	borrowers per scheme after two years of operation, with wide variation by town size
    32	(Carraway Trust, 2022). The same survey reported a median household saving of GBP 60 a year
    33	among borrowers who answered its questionnaire.
    34	Repeat borrowing, the share of borrowers who borrow more than once, is often used as a sign
    35	that a scheme has become part of household routines. It was 34 percent at the Harwick Tool
    36	Library in its second year (Pemberton and Shah, 2021) and 39 percent at the Otterburn Share
    37	Shed (Lindqvist, 2023). Damage rates reported by tool libraries usually fall between 2 and 5
    38	percent of loans, with power tools at the upper end of that range (Odum, 2020).
    39	Estimates of environmental benefit vary more widely. Faraday and Mbeki (2022) estimated that
    40	a large urban scheme avoided 52 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in a year, but noted
    41	that the result depended heavily on what borrowers said they would otherwise have bought. No
    42	published study that we are aware of has followed a scheme in a town of Brackenford's size
    43	for more than one year.
    44	
    45	3 Methods
    46	3.1 The scheme
    47	At launch the catalogue held 164 items, chosen by library staff after a public consultation,
    48	and by March 2025 it had grown to 236 items. Standard members paid between GBP 1 and GBP 6
    49	per loan, depending on the item, while members receiving Council Tax Reduction borrowed free
    50	of charge. Staff checked each item on return against a written checklist and recorded any
    51	damage on the loan record.
    52	3.2 Membership and loan records
    53	We analysed the anonymised membership and loan records for the whole pilot period. Each loan
    54	record held the item, the branch, the dates of issue and return, the fee paid and any damage
    55	recorded at return. Membership records held the branch of registration and the home
    56	postcode, which we used to assign each borrower to a deprivation quintile of the Index of
    57	Multiple Deprivation.
    58	3.3 Borrower survey
    59	In February 2025 we sent an online survey to all 1,421 members who had borrowed at least one
    60	item, and paper copies were offered at all three branches. The survey asked what borrowers
    61	had used items for, what they would have done without the scheme, and how much they thought
    62	they had saved. It received 426 responses, a response rate of 30 percent.
    63	3.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
    64	We estimated avoided purchases by applying the share of survey respondents who said they
    65	would otherwise have bought each type of item to the number of different members who
    66	borrowed that type of item, so that repeat loans of the same item by the same member were
    67	counted once. Emissions were then estimated from the weight and main material of each type
    68	of item, using published factors for the manufacture of household equipment (Faraday and
    69	Mbeki, 2022).
    70	
    71	3.5 Analysis
    72	We report counts and percentages for the whole pilot and for each year, where year one runs
    73	from April 2023 to March 2024 and year two from April 2024 to March 2025. Before analysis we
    74	removed 203 loan records that staff had created to test the booking system or that had been
    75	recorded twice because of a software fault in the summer of 2023.
    76	4 Results
    77	4.1 Membership and reach
    78	By the end of March 2025, 1,936 people had registered as borrowers across the three
    79	branches. Just over half registered at Central, which is the largest branch and the only one
    80	open on Sundays (Table 1).
    81	Table 1. Registered borrowers by branch of registration, April 2023 to March 2025
    82	Branch Registered borrowers Share of registrations Concession members
    83	Central 1,012 52 percent 198
    84	Eastgate 538 28 percent 171
    85	Millbrook 386 20 percent 94
    86	All branches 1,936 100 percent 463
    87	Of the 1,490 borrowers with a usable home postcode, 611 (41 percent) lived in neighbourhoods
    88	in the two most deprived quintiles. This is close to the 40 percent of Brackenford residents
    89	who live in those neighbourhoods. The remaining 446 registrations had no usable postcode,
    90	mostly because borrowers had registered with a work address, and they are not included in
    91	this figure.
    92	
    93	4.2 Loans and repeat use
    94	Borrowers made 5,712 loans over the two years, 2,214 in year one and 3,498 in year two. This
    95	rise of 58 percent came mostly from Central and Eastgate, where reservations could be
    96	collected on the same day from the spring of 2024. Loans peaked in May and August of each
    97	year and were lowest in January.
    98	Of the 1,936 registered borrowers, 1,421 made at least one loan. Among these active
    99	borrowers, 668 borrowed more than once. That is a repeat borrowing rate of 47 percent, and
   100	it was 53 percent among those who joined in year one and 38 percent among those who joined
   101	in year two, who had less time to borrow again.
   102	The ten most borrowed items accounted for 45 percent of all loans (Table 2). Decorating and
   103	cleaning equipment was borrowed most in spring, and garden and outdoor equipment in summer.
   104	Table 2. The ten most borrowed items, April 2023 to March 2025
   105	Item Loans Share of all loans
   106	Carpet cleaner 418 7.3 percent
   107	Pressure washer 377 6.6 percent
   108	Hedge trimmer 301 5.3 percent
   109	Sewing machine 266 4.7 percent
   110	Wallpaper steamer 244 4.3 percent
   111	Gazebo 231 4.0 percent
   112	Cordless drill 219 3.8 percent
   113	Projector and screen 187 3.3 percent
   114	Four-person tent 171 3.0 percent
   115	Paint sprayer 158 2.8 percent
   116	
   117	4.3 Savings to households
   118	Survey respondents estimated that borrowing instead of buying or hiring had saved their
   119	household a median of GBP 85 over the previous twelve months. Savings were largest among
   120	those who had borrowed decorating equipment, for whom the median was GBP 120. These
   121	estimates are self-reported, and respondents may have overstated what they would otherwise
   122	have spent.
   123	Asked what they would have done without the scheme, 62 percent of respondents said they
   124	would have bought the item, 21 percent would have borrowed it from friends or family, 9
   125	percent would have hired it and 8 percent would have gone without.
   126	4.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
   127	Applying these answers to the 1,820 combinations of member and item type in the loan
   128	records, we estimate that the pilot avoided the purchase of about 1,130 items with a
   129	combined weight of 14.6 tonnes. These avoided purchases correspond to around 38 tonnes of
   130	carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years, mostly from power tools and garden machinery.
   131	The estimate is an upper bound, because it assumes that every respondent who said they would
   132	have bought an item would in fact have done so.
   133	
   134	4.5 Condition of returned items
   135	Staff recorded damage at return on 3.1 percent of loans. A further 19 items were lost or
   136	never returned, equal to 0.3 percent of loans. Repairs and replacements cost GBP 2,460 over
   137	the two years, or about 43 pence per loan. Damage was most common for power tools and garden
   138	equipment (Table 3).
   139	Table 3. Loans with damage recorded at return, by item category
   140	Category Loans Returned damaged Damage rate
   141	Power tools 1,240 64 5.2 percent
   142	Garden equipment 1,105 47 4.3 percent
   143	Cleaning equipment 1,032 29 2.8 percent
   144	Sewing and craft 602 10 1.7 percent
   145	Camping and events 894 19 2.1 percent
   146	Electronics 839 8 1.0 percent
   147	All categories 5,712 177 3.1 percent
   148	5 Discussion
   149	The pilot reached more people than most schemes of its kind, and registrations were well
   150	above the median reported for English schemes after two years. Use also grew steadily
   151	through the second year. Repeat borrowing was higher than in the two schemes reviewed in
   152	Section 2, which suggests that a core group of households has made borrowing a habit.
   153	Borrowers' estimates of what they saved were larger than in the national survey, but they
   154	remain small in relation to household budgets. The scheme's main value to many members may
   155	lie less in money saved than in access to equipment they could not store or could not
   156	justify buying.
   157	
   158	The environmental benefits are real but uncertain. Our estimate of avoided emissions depends
   159	on what borrowers said they would otherwise have done, and on factors for manufacturing
   160	emissions that are themselves approximate.
   161	6 Limitations
   162	The evaluation had no comparison group, so we cannot say how many borrowers would have found
   163	other ways to share or hire equipment. The survey reached only 30 percent of active
   164	borrowers, and those who responded may have been more positive about the scheme than those
   165	who did not. Damage was recorded by staff at the point of return, so faults found later,
   166	when items were next checked or lent, are not counted. The evaluation did not assess effects
   167	on local retailers, such as hardware and DIY shops, or on commercial hire firms.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	The Library of Things pilot met its aims for reach and regular use, and it delivered savings
   170	and environmental benefits that, while uncertain in size, point in the right direction. We
   171	recommend that Brackenford Libraries continue the scheme, record damage throughout an item's
   172	life rather than only at return, and use loan data to guide which items are bought.
   173	
   174	Acknowledgements
   175	We thank the staff of Central, Eastgate and Millbrook libraries, the borrowers who completed
   176	the survey, and the Halden Foundation, which funded both the pilot and this evaluation.
   177	References
   178	Carraway Trust (2022) Libraries of things in England: a survey of 14 schemes. Carraway
   179	Trust.
   180	Faraday, L and Mbeki, T (2022) Counting the carbon in shared equipment. Journal of Circular
   181	Economy Studies, 4(2), 51 to 66.
   182	Lindqvist, A (2023) The Otterburn Share Shed: second-year review. Otterburn Community Trust.
   183	Odum, K (2020) Wear and tear in tool libraries. Community Lending Review, 7, 12 to 19.
   184	Pemberton, J and Shah, R (2021) Who borrows tools? Evidence from the Harwick Tool Library.
   185	Local Economy Notes, 15, 3 to 11.

results.answer:
The pilot’s main findings were:

- It reached a substantial number of residents: by March 2025, 1,936 people had registered as borrowers.
- Use grew strongly: there were 5,712 loans over two years, with loans rising by 58% from year one to year two.
- Repeat use was fairly strong: 47% of active borrowers borrowed more than once.
- Borrowers reported modest financial savings: the median estimated saving was GBP 85 over the previous 12 months.
- The scheme likely reduced purchases and waste: it is estimated to have avoided about 1,130 item purchases and around 38 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.
- Most items were returned in good condition: damage was recorded on 3.1% of loans, and losses were rare.
- Access was reasonably broad: registrations from deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with the town’s population share.

Overall, the report concluded that the pilot met its aims for reach and regular use, delivered savings and environmental benefits, and recommended continuing the scheme with improved damage recording and item selection.

ANSWER: The Library of Things pilot was judged successful overall: it attracted nearly 2,000 borrowers, use grew strongly, repeat borrowing was solid, borrowers reported modest savings, the scheme appears to have reduced purchases and emissions, and most items were returned in good condition.

   151	through the second year. Repeat borrowing was higher than in the two schemes reviewed in
   152	Section 2, which suggests that a core group of households has made borrowing a habit.
   153	Borrowers' estimates of what they saved were larger than in the national survey, but they
   154	remain small in relation to household budgets. The scheme's main value to many members may
   155	lie less in money saved than in access to equipment they could not store or could not
   156	justify buying.
   157	
   158	The environmental benefits are real but uncertain. Our estimate of avoided emissions depends
   159	on what borrowers said they would otherwise have done, and on factors for manufacturing
   160	emissions that are themselves approximate.
   161	6 Limitations
   162	The evaluation had no comparison group, so we cannot say how many borrowers would have found
   163	other ways to share or hire equipment. The survey reached only 30 percent of active
   164	borrowers, and those who responded may have been more positive about the scheme than those
   165	who did not. Damage was recorded by staff at the point of return, so faults found later,
   166	when items were next checked or lent, are not counted. The evaluation did not assess effects
   167	on local retailers, such as hardware and DIY shops, or on commercial hire firms.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	The Library of Things pilot met its aims for reach and regular use, and it delivered savings
   170	and environmental benefits that, while uncertain in size, point in the right direction. We
   171	recommend that Brackenford Libraries continue the scheme, record damage throughout an item's
   172	life rather than only at return, and use loan data to guide which items are bought.
   173	
   174	Acknowledgements
   175	We thank the staff of Central, Eastgate and Millbrook libraries, the borrowers who completed
   176	the survey, and the Halden Foundation, which funded both the pilot and this evaluation.
   177	References
   178	Carraway Trust (2022) Libraries of things in England: a survey of 14 schemes. Carraway
   179	Trust.
   180	Faraday, L and Mbeki, T (2022) Counting the carbon in shared equipment. Journal of Circular
   181	Economy Studies, 4(2), 51 to 66.
   182	Lindqvist, A (2023) The Otterburn Share Shed: second-year review. Otterburn Community Trust.
   183	Odum, K (2020) Wear and tear in tool libraries. Community Lending Review, 7, 12 to 19.
   184	Pemberton, J and Shah, R (2021) Who borrows tools? Evidence from the Harwick Tool Library.
   185	Local Economy Notes, 15, 3 to 11.
results.answer:
The main findings were:

- The pilot attracted strong uptake: almost 2,000 residents registered, and loans grew by 64 percent between the first and second years.
- It reached a broad mix of residents: registrations from deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with their share of the town’s population.
- It encouraged repeat use: 47 percent of active borrowers borrowed more than once.
- Borrowers reported modest savings: the median estimated household saving was GBP 85 over the previous 12 months.
- Environmental benefits were positive but uncertain: the evaluation estimated about 38 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent avoided over two years.
- Most items were returned in good condition: damage was recorded on 3.1 percent of loans, with 0.3 percent lost or never returned.
- The report concluded the scheme met its aims for reach and regular use, and recommended that it continue, with improved damage recording and a better system for choosing new items.

ANSWER: The pilot was successful overall: it reached nearly 2,000 residents, saw strong and growing use, engaged deprived neighbourhoods proportionately, produced modest household savings, and likely reduced waste and emissions, while keeping damage and loss relatively low.

results.answer:
The pilot evaluation found that the Library of Things scheme had grown strongly and was being used by a broad group of residents:

- Almost 2,000 residents registered as borrowers over the first two years.
- Loans increased by 64% overall between year one and year two.
- By March 2025, 1,936 people had registered, and 1,421 of them had made at least one loan.
- Repeat borrowing was fairly common: 47% of active borrowers borrowed more than once.
- The scheme appears to have produced practical savings for users: the median estimated household saving was GBP 85 over the previous 12 months.
- It also reduced consumption: the evaluation estimates about 1,130 item purchases were avoided, saving around 38 tonnes of CO2e over two years.
- Operationally, the scheme held up well: damage was recorded on only 3.1% of loans, with low repair and replacement costs.
- The report’s overall conclusion was that the scheme’s main value may be access to equipment people could not store or justify buying, not just money saved.

ANSWER: The main findings were that the pilot attracted nearly 2,000 borrowers, loans grew strongly over the two years, many users borrowed repeatedly, the scheme saved households money and avoided some purchases and emissions, and returned items were generally in good condition with low damage and repair costs.

     1	Warmer homes, lower bills? Evaluation of the Kestle Bay Community Heat Pump Programme, 2022 to 2024
     2	Tressider Energy Research, for Kestle Bay Community Energy. Final report, March 2025.
     3	Abstract
     4	Kestle Bay Community Energy, a community benefit society, ran a programme between October
     5	2022 and September 2024 to help owner-occupiers on the Kestle Bay peninsula replace
     6	fossil-fuel heating with air-source heat pumps. The programme combined group purchasing,
     7	free home surveys and a grant of GBP 6,000 per home. This evaluation draws on the society's
     8	records, smart meter data, temperature loggers and a follow-up survey of residents.
     9	Household energy bills fell by 21 percent on average after installation, and homes were
    10	warmer in winter. Emissions from heating fell substantially. Most residents were satisfied
    11	with their systems, although around one in ten reported a fault in the first year. The
    12	programme offers a model that other community energy groups could adapt, provided that
    13	enough installer capacity can be secured.
    14	1 Introduction
    15	Heating accounts for most household energy use and emissions in rural and coastal areas,
    16	where many homes are not connected to the gas grid and rely on heating oil or bottled gas.
    17	Air-source heat pumps can cut both bills and emissions, but take-up has been slow, held back
    18	by upfront cost, uncertainty about how well they work in older homes and a shortage of
    19	trusted installers.
    20	
    21	Kestle Bay Community Energy set out to tackle these barriers locally. It recruited
    22	households through village halls and word of mouth, arranged free home surveys, negotiated a
    23	group price with two installers and administered a grant funded by the Coastal Communities
    24	Net Zero Fund. This report evaluates the programme's uptake, its effects on energy bills,
    25	indoor temperatures and emissions, and residents' experience of their new heating systems.
    26	2 Background and previous studies
    27	Field trials of air-source heat pumps in existing homes have reported reductions in annual
    28	energy bills of between 8 and 25 percent, with the largest reductions in homes that
    29	previously used heating oil or electric storage heaters (Ashworth and Kaur, 2021). Results
    30	depend strongly on the efficiency achieved in practice, which tends to be lower in homes
    31	with small radiators or poor insulation.
    32	Community-led schemes have reported mixed uptake. In the Lowmoor scheme, 29 percent of
    33	households that registered an interest went on to have a heat pump installed (Lowmoor
    34	Energy, 2022). Studies of comfort after installation have found mean living-room
    35	temperatures rising by between 0.5 and 1.0 deg C (Brennan, 2020). Greaves and Tan (2023)
    36	estimated typical savings of 1.8 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per home per year where
    37	a heat pump replaces a gas boiler. In a national panel of heat pump users, 79 percent said
    38	they were satisfied with their system (Heat Pump Users Panel, 2022).
    39	
    40	3 Methods
    41	3.1 The programme
    42	Households could register an interest online or at one of eleven drop-in sessions held in
    43	village halls. Each registered household was offered a free home survey by an independent
    44	assessor, who checked insulation, radiators and the electricity supply. Households that went
    45	ahead received a grant of GBP 6,000 towards the installed cost and could borrow the
    46	remainder through an interest-free loan arranged by the society. Two installers were
    47	appointed after a tender in the summer of 2022.
    48	3.2 Data sources
    49	We used four sources: the society's records of registrations, surveys and installations;
    50	half-hourly smart meter data for electricity and gas, shared with the householder's consent;
    51	installers' records of costs and faults; and a follow-up survey of residents twelve months
    52	after installation. Temperature loggers were placed in the living rooms of 48 homes that
    53	volunteered, recording every thirty minutes for one winter before and one winter after
    54	installation.
    55	3.3 Energy bills
    56	For homes with a full year of meter data before and after installation, we calculated annual
    57	spending on electricity and all heating fuels. To remove the effect of price changes, both
    58	years were valued at the unit rates and standing charges in force in October 2023. Use of
    59	heating oil and bottled gas was taken from delivery records.
    60	
    61	3.4 Emissions
    62	Emissions from heating were modelled from metered fuel and electricity use, using the
    63	government's 2023 conversion factors for each fuel. The same factor for grid electricity was
    64	used for both years, so the results do not reflect any further decarbonisation of the grid.
    65	3.5 Resident survey and temperatures
    66	The follow-up survey asked about comfort, running costs, problems and overall satisfaction,
    67	and was sent to all households with an installation. Temperatures were summarised as the
    68	mean living-room temperature between 1 December and 28 February in each winter.
    69	4 Results
    70	4.1 Uptake
    71	Between October 2022 and September 2024, 597 households registered an interest, 318 received
    72	a home survey and 214 had a heat pump installed. This conversion rate of 36 percent from
    73	registration to installation is above that reported for the Lowmoor scheme. Most households
    74	that dropped out after the survey cited the cost remaining after the grant, and a smaller
    75	number were advised that their home needed insulation work first.
    76	Table 1. Households at each stage, by main heating fuel before the programme
    77	Main heating fuel Registered interest Home survey Installed
    78	Mains gas 392 196 121
    79	Heating oil 128 79 63
    80	Electric storage heaters 51 29 21
    81	Bottled gas (LPG) 26 14 9
    82	All households 597 318 214
    83	
    84	4.2 Energy bills
    85	Complete meter data for a full year before and after installation were available for 162
    86	homes. In these homes, mean annual energy spend fell from GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818, valued at
    87	October 2023 prices. This fall of 17 percent, or GBP 372 a year, was larger in homes that
    88	had previously used heating oil than in homes that had used mains gas.
    89	Savings also varied with the construction of the home (Table 2). For the 52 homes without
    90	complete meter data, installers' estimates suggest similar savings, but these could not be
    91	checked.
    92	Table 2. Mean annual energy spend before and after installation, by wall type, at October
    93	2023 prices
    94	Wall type Homes Before (GBP) After (GBP) Change
    95	Solid wall, built before 1919 38 2,640 2,455 -7 percent
    96	Cavity wall, insulated 81 2,050 1,600 -22 percent
    97	Cavity wall, not insulated 27 2,180 1,844 -15 percent
    98	Built after 1990 16 1,847 1,365 -26 percent
    99	All homes with full meter data 162 2,190 1,818 -17 percent
   100	
   101	4.3 Indoor temperatures
   102	In the 48 homes with temperature loggers, the mean living-room temperature from December to
   103	February rose by 1.6 deg C, from 17.9 deg C before installation to 19.5 deg C after. This
   104	gain was largest in homes that had relied on electric storage heaters, which had often been
   105	the coldest before the programme. Fewer residents reported shutting off rooms in winter to
   106	save money. The comparison is not adjusted for weather, and the second winter was on average
   107	1.1 deg C milder outdoors than the first.
   108	4.4 Emissions
   109	Modelled emissions from heating fell by a mean of 2.3 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent
   110	per home per year, a reduction of 61 percent. Across all 214 installations, this amounts to
   111	about 490 tonnes a year. These savings were roughly twice as large in oil-heated homes as in
   112	gas-heated homes, reflecting the higher carbon content of heating oil.
   113	
   114	4.5 Residents' experience
   115	Of the 214 households with an installation, 171 answered the follow-up survey, a response
   116	rate of 80 percent. Among respondents, 84 percent were satisfied or very satisfied with
   117	their heat pump, and 77 percent said their home was more comfortable than before.
   118	Twenty-three households, 11 percent of those with an installation, reported a fault in the
   119	first year (Table 3). Most faults were fixed within a week, but three households were
   120	without heating for more than five days.
   121	Table 3. Faults reported in the first year after installation, by type
   122	Type of fault Households Median days to fix
   123	Controls or thermostat 9 2
   124	Hot water cylinder 6 4
   125	Outdoor unit 4 6
   126	Electrical supply 2 3
   127	Refrigerant leak 2 9
   128	All faults 23 3
   129	5 Discussion
   130	The programme turned a larger share of interested households into installations than
   131	comparable community schemes, which suggests that free surveys and a trusted local
   132	organisation can overcome some of the barriers to take-up. The cost remaining after the
   133	grant was the main reason for dropping out, and future phases may need larger grants or
   134	loans for households on low incomes.
   135	The fall in bills is within the range reported in field trials, and the larger savings in
   136	oil-heated homes match earlier findings. Savings in older solid-wall homes were smaller,
   137	which supports the case for combining heat pumps with insulation where that is affordable.
   138	
   139	6 Limitations
   140	There was no comparison group of homes that kept their old heating, so changes in bills and
   141	temperatures may partly reflect other changes in households. Meter data were complete for
   142	only 162 of the 214 homes, and temperature loggers were placed in only 48 volunteer homes,
   143	which may not be typical. Emissions were modelled rather than measured. The follow-up survey
   144	was carried out by the society itself, which may have encouraged favourable answers.
   145	7 Conclusions
   146	The Kestle Bay programme shows that a community energy group can deliver heat pumps at scale
   147	in an area with many older and off-grid homes. Households saved money and were warmer, and
   148	emissions from heating fell sharply. We recommend that the next phase gives priority to
   149	oil-heated homes, offers insulation alongside heat pumps in solid-wall homes, and secures
   150	more installer capacity.
   151	Acknowledgements
   152	We thank the residents who shared their meter data and answered the survey, the staff and
   153	volunteers of Kestle Bay Community Energy, and the Coastal Communities Net Zero Fund.
   154	References
   155	Ashworth, P and Kaur, S (2021) Heat pumps in existing homes: results of a field trial.
   156	Building Energy Research, 12, 101 to 118.
   157	Brennan, M (2020) Comfort after retrofit. Housing and Health Review, 9, 44 to 52.
   158	Greaves, H and Tan, W (2023) Carbon savings from domestic heat pumps. Energy Policy Notes,
   159	31, 7 to 15.
   160	Heat Pump Users Panel (2022) Annual survey of heat pump users. Heat Pump Users Panel.
   161	Lowmoor Energy (2022) The Lowmoor heat pump scheme: final report. Lowmoor Energy
   162	Cooperative.

results.answer:
The main findings of the Kestle Bay community heat pump programme evaluation were:

- Households’ energy bills fell after installation: among homes with full meter data, average annual spend dropped from **GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818** — a **17%** fall, or **GBP 372 a year**.
- Homes were warmer in winter: in the monitored homes, mean living-room temperature rose by **1.6°C**.
- Heating emissions fell sharply: modelled emissions dropped by **2.3 tonnes of CO2e per home per year**, a **61%** reduction, or about **490 tonnes a year** across all installations.
- Uptake was relatively strong: **214 homes** got heat pumps out of **597** expressing interest, a **36% conversion rate**.
- Residents were mostly positive: **84%** of survey respondents were satisfied or very satisfied, and **77%** said their home was more comfortable.
- Problems did occur: about **11%** of installed households reported a fault in the first year, though most were fixed quickly.
- The programme’s biggest barrier was cost, especially the amount remaining after the grant; the report suggests larger grants or loans may be needed for lower-income households.

In short, the evaluation found that the programme successfully delivered heat pumps at scale and brought lower bills, warmer homes, and lower emissions, with some installation faults and affordability barriers remaining.

ANSWER: The evaluation found that the programme delivered heat pumps at scale and was generally successful: bills fell, homes became warmer, emissions dropped sharply, most residents were satisfied, but upfront cost remained the main barrier and about one in ten households reported a first-year fault.

    67	and was sent to all households with an installation. Temperatures were summarised as the
    68	mean living-room temperature between 1 December and 28 February in each winter.

    70	4.1 Uptake
    71	Between October 2022 and September 2024, 597 households registered an interest, 318 received
    72	a home survey and 214 had a heat pump installed. This conversion rate of 36 percent from
    73	registration to installation is above that reported for the Lowmoor scheme. Most households
    74	that dropped out after the survey cited the cost remaining after the grant, and a smaller
    75	number were advised that their home needed insulation work first.

    78	Mains gas 392 196 121
    79	Heating oil 128 79 63
    80	Electric storage heaters 51 29 21
    81	Bottled gas (LPG) 26 14 9
    82	All households 597 318 214
    83	
    84	4.2 Energy bills
    85	Complete meter data for a full year before and after installation were available for 162
    86	homes. In these homes, mean annual energy spend fell from GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818, valued at
    87	October 2023 prices. This fall of 17 percent, or GBP 372 a year, was larger in homes that
    88	had previously used heating oil than in homes that had used mains gas.
    89	Savings also varied with the construction of the home (Table 2). For the 52 homes without
    90	complete meter data, installers' estimates suggest similar savings, but these could not be
    91	checked.

    93	2023 prices
    94	Wall type Homes Before (GBP) After (GBP) Change
    95	Solid wall, built before 1919 38 2,640 2,455 -7 percent
    96	Cavity wall, insulated 81 2,050 1,600 -22 percent
    97	Cavity wall, not insulated 27 2,180 1,844 -15 percent
    98	Built after 1990 16 1,847 1,365 -26 percent

   103	February rose by 1.6 deg C, from 17.9 deg C before installation to 19.5 deg C after. This
   104	gain was largest in homes that had relied on electric storage heaters, which had often been
   105	the coldest before the programme. Fewer residents reported shutting off rooms in winter to
   106	save money. The comparison is not adjusted for weather, and the second winter was on average
   107	1.1 deg C milder outdoors than the first.
   108	4.4 Emissions
   109	Modelled emissions from heating fell by a mean of 2.3 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent
   110	per home per year, a reduction of 61 percent. Across all 214 installations, this amounts to
   111	about 490 tonnes a year. These savings were roughly twice as large in oil-heated homes as in
   112	gas-heated homes, reflecting the higher carbon content of heating oil.
   113	
   114	4.5 Residents' experience
   115	Of the 214 households with an installation, 171 answered the follow-up survey, a response
   116	rate of 80 percent. Among respondents, 84 percent were satisfied or very satisfied with
   117	their heat pump, and 77 percent said their home was more comfortable than before.
   118	Twenty-three households, 11 percent of those with an installation, reported a fault in the
   119	first year (Table 3). Most faults were fixed within a week, but three households were
   120	without heating for more than five days.

   122	Type of fault Households Median days to fix
   123	Controls or thermostat 9 2
   124	Hot water cylinder 6 4

   127	Refrigerant leak 2 9
   128	All faults 23 3

   130	The programme turned a larger share of interested households into installations than
   131	comparable community schemes, which suggests that free surveys and a trusted local
   132	organisation can overcome some of the barriers to take-up. The cost remaining after the
   133	grant was the main reason for dropping out, and future phases may need larger grants or
   134	loans for households on low incomes.

   136	oil-heated homes match earlier findings. Savings in older solid-wall homes were smaller,
   137	which supports the case for combining heat pumps with insulation where that is affordable.

   141	temperatures may partly reflect other changes in households. Meter data were complete for

results.answer:
The main findings of the Kestle Bay community heat pump programme evaluation were:

- The programme achieved strong uptake: 597 households registered interest and 214 installed heat pumps, a 36% conversion from registration to installation.
- Household energy bills fell after installation:
  - for the 162 homes with full meter data, mean annual energy spend fell from £2,190 to £1,818, a 17% reduction;
  - the abstract reports an average fall of 21%.
- Homes were warmer in winter:
  - in the 48 monitored homes, mean living-room temperature rose from 17.9°C to 19.5°C, an increase of 1.6°C.
- Heating emissions fell sharply:
  - modelled emissions dropped by 2.3 tonnes of CO2e per home per year, a 61% reduction;
  - across all installations, that was about 490 tonnes a year.
- Residents were generally positive:
  - 84% of survey respondents were satisfied or very satisfied;
  - 77% said their home was more comfortable than before.
- There were some problems:
  - 11% of installed households reported a fault in the first year, though most were fixed quickly.
- The report’s overall conclusion was that the scheme shows community energy groups can deliver heat pumps at scale, but future phases need more installer capacity, and likely larger support for lower-income households and insulation in solid-wall homes.

ANSWER: The programme increased uptake of heat pumps, cut average household energy bills, made homes warmer, sharply reduced heating emissions, and was mostly well received by residents, though some households had first-year faults and the report says future schemes need more installer capacity and better support for higher remaining costs and insulation in older homes.

The main findings of the Kestle Bay Community Heat Pump Programme evaluation were:

- Uptake was strong: between October 2022 and September 2024, 597 households registered an interest, 318 received a home survey, and 214 had a heat pump installed.
- Energy bills fell: in the 162 homes with full meter data, mean annual energy spend fell from GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818, a fall of 17 percent, or GBP 372 a year.
- Homes were warmer: in the 48 homes with temperature loggers, mean living-room temperature rose by 1.6 deg C, from 17.9 deg C to 19.5 deg C.
- Emissions dropped sharply: modelled heating emissions fell by a mean of 2.3 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per home per year, a reduction of 61 percent, or about 490 tonnes a year across all 214 installations.
- Residents were mostly satisfied: among the 171 survey respondents, 84 percent were satisfied or very satisfied, and 77 percent said their home was more comfortable than before.
- Around one in ten reported faults in the first year: 23 households, 11 percent of those with an installation, reported a fault, with most fixed within a week.

The report concludes that the programme “shows that a community energy group can deliver heat pumps at scale in an area with many older and off-grid homes,” and recommends prioritising oil-heated homes, offering insulation alongside heat pumps in solid-wall homes, and securing more installer capacity.

ANSWER: The programme had strong uptake, with 214 installations from 597 interested households; it reduced average annual energy bills by 17 percent (from GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818), raised indoor temperatures by 1.6 deg C, cut heating emissions by 61 percent (about 2.3 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per home per year), and most residents were satisfied, though 11 percent reported a first-year fault.

results.answer:
The evaluation found that the Kestle Bay community heat pump programme:

- Successfully delivered heat pumps at scale: 597 households registered, 318 had a survey, and 214 had an installation.
- Reduced household energy bills: for the 162 homes with full meter data, mean annual spend fell from GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818, a 17 percent drop.
- Made homes warmer: in the 48 monitored homes, mean winter living-room temperature rose by 1.6°C, from 17.9°C to 19.5°C.
- Cut emissions substantially: modelled heating emissions fell by 2.3 tonnes of CO2e per home per year, a 61 percent reduction, about 490 tonnes a year across all installations.
- Was well received by residents: 84 percent of survey respondents were satisfied or very satisfied, and 77 percent said their home was more comfortable.
- Had some reliability issues: 11 percent reported a fault in the first year, though most were fixed quickly.
- Faced affordability barriers: the remaining cost after the grant was the main reason some households dropped out, suggesting future phases may need larger grants or loans for lower-income households.

ANSWER: The programme was judged a success overall: it achieved substantial uptake, cut bills and emissions, warmed homes, and left most residents satisfied, but upfront cost remained a key barrier and some first-year faults occurred.

  p.1 Warmer homes, lower bills? Evaluation of the Kestle Bay Community Heat Pump Programme, 2022 to 2024
  p.1 Tressider Energy Research, for Kestle Bay Community Energy. Final report, March 2025.
  p.1 Kestle Bay Community Energy, a community benefit society, ran a programme between October 2022 and September 2024 to help owner-occupiers on the Kestle Bay peninsula replace fossil-fuel heating with air-source heat pumps. The programme combined group purchasing, free home surveys and a grant of GBP 6,000 per home. This evaluation draws on the society's records, smart meter data, temperature loggers and a follow-up survey of residents. Household energy bills fell by 21 percent on average after installation, and homes were warmer in winter. Emissions from heating fell substantially. Most residents were satisfied with their systems, although around one in ten reported a fault in the first year. The programme offers a model that other community energy groups could adapt, provided that enough installer capacity can be secured.
  p.1 Heating accounts for most household energy use and emissions in rural and coastal areas, where many homes are not connected to the gas grid and rely on heating oil or bottled gas. Air-source heat pumps can cut both bills and emissions, but take-up has been slow, held back by upfront cost, uncertainty about how well they work in older homes and a shortage of trusted installers.
  p.2 Kestle Bay Community Energy set out to tackle these barriers locally. It recruited households through village halls and word of mouth, arranged free home surveys, negotiated a group price with two installers and administered a grant funded by the Coastal Communities Net Zero Fund. This report evaluates the programme's uptake, its effects on energy bills, indoor temperatures and emissions, and residents' experience of their new heating systems.
  p.2 2 Background and previous studies
  p.2 Field trials of air-source heat pumps in existing homes have reported reductions in annual energy bills of between 8 and 25 percent, with the largest reductions in homes that previously used heating oil or electric storage heaters (Ashworth and Kaur, 2021). Results depend strongly on the efficiency achieved in practice, which tends to be lower in homes with small radiators or poor insulation.
  p.2 Community-led schemes have reported mixed uptake. In the Lowmoor scheme, 29 percent of households that registered an interest went on to have a heat pump installed (Lowmoor Energy, 2022). Studies of comfort after installation have found mean living-room temperatures rising by between 0.5 and 1.0 deg C (Brennan, 2020). Greaves and Tan (2023) estimated typical savings of 1.8 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per home per year where a heat pump replaces a gas boiler. In a national panel of heat pump users, 79 percent said they were satisfied with their system (Heat Pump Users Panel, 2022).

# Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024

## Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024

Present: Rosa Penhallow (chair), Daniel Kitto, Meera Joshi, Tom Rowe and Ellen Vosper (programme manager). Apologies: Gareth Lobb.

## Progress

Ellen reported that the first phase closed in September with 214 installations. Installers now report a median of 9 weeks between the home survey and the installation date, down from 14 weeks in the first year of the programme.

## Installers

Brightwater Heating withdrew from the programme in August because of staff shortages, leaving Pellow and Sons as the only appointed installer. The board agreed to run a new tender in January to appoint at least one more installer before phase two begins.

## Complaints

Six formal complaints were received in 2024, four of them about installation delays and two about the condition of gardens after outdoor units were fitted. All have been resolved.

## Phase two

The board agreed a target of 150 further installations by March 2026, with priority for homes heated by oil or bottled gas. It also agreed to cap the householder contribution at GBP 4,000 for households receiving means-tested benefits, with the society's hardship fund meeting the rest of the cost.

## Actions

Ellen to draft the installer tender by 12 December. Daniel to ask the Coastal Communities Net Zero Fund whether the grant can stay at GBP 6,000 per home in phase two. Meera to update the website with the new waiting times.

     1	Library of Things pilot: briefing for the Communities Committee
     2	
     3	From the Head of Libraries, Brackenford Council. For the committee meeting on 18 November 2025.
     4	
     5	Purpose
     6	
     7	This briefing summarises the independent evaluation of the Library of Things pilot by Northfold Social Research and sets out the library service's proposals for the scheme's future.
     8	
     9	What the evaluation found
    10	
    11	The pilot exceeded its target of 1,500 registered borrowers, and use grew in the second year. Borrowers reported that they saved money, and most items came back in good condition. The service accepts the evaluation's findings, with one exception set out below.
    12	
    13	Damage to items
    14	
    15	Our own repair log records damage on 6.8 percent of loans, more than twice the evaluation's figure. The difference arises because the evaluation counted only damage noted by staff when an item was returned, while the repair log also includes faults found at the next safety check or by the next borrower. We consider the repair log the better measure of the cost of wear and tear.
    16	
    17	Proposals
    18	
    19	We propose to continue the scheme for a further three years and to open a fourth collection point at Northfield library from April 2026, at an estimated additional cost of GBP 31,000 a year. From January 2026, borrowers of power tools would pay a refundable deposit of GBP 10, which the service expects to reduce damage and late returns. Members receiving Council Tax Reduction would continue to borrow free of charge.
    20	
    21	Recommendation
    22	
    23	The committee is asked to approve the continuation and extension of the Library of Things as set out above, funded from the libraries budget and from loan fees.
     1	Borrowing instead of buying: evaluation of the Brackenford Library of Things pilot, April 2023 to March 2025
     2	Northfold Social Research, for Brackenford Libraries. Final report, September 2025.
     3	Abstract
     4	The Brackenford Library of Things lends household tools and equipment from three branch
     5	libraries for a small fee. This report evaluates the first two years of the pilot, from
     6	April 2023 to March 2025, using membership and loan records, a survey of borrowers and the
     7	checks that staff make when items are returned. Almost 2,000 residents registered as
     8	borrowers, and loans grew by 64 percent between the first and second years. Borrowers
     9	reported modest savings, and most items came back in good condition. Registrations from
    10	deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with their share of the town's population. We
    11	recommend that the scheme continues, with changes to how damage is recorded and how new
    12	items are chosen.
    13	1 Introduction
    14	Libraries of things apply the familiar library model to objects that households need only
    15	occasionally, such as drills, gazebos and sewing machines. Their supporters argue that
    16	borrowing saves money, reduces the number of rarely used items that people buy, and brings
    17	people into libraries who would not otherwise visit.
    18	Brackenford Libraries opened its Library of Things in April 2023 with a grant of GBP 96,000
    19	from the Halden Foundation, which also funded this evaluation. The pilot ran from three of
    20	the town's seven branch libraries: Central, Eastgate and Millbrook.
    21	
    22	Items could be reserved online and collected from any of the three branches, and loans
    23	lasted up to seven days. This report sets out what the pilot achieved against the aims
    24	agreed with the funder: to reach a broad range of residents, to build regular use, to save
    25	households money and to reduce waste. Section 2 summarises earlier evaluations of similar
    26	schemes, Section 3 describes our methods, Section 4 presents the results, and Sections 5 to
    27	7 discuss them.
    28	2 Previous studies
    29	Published evaluations of libraries of things are few, and most describe a single scheme in
    30	its first years. A survey of 14 schemes in England found a median of 1,150 registered
    31	borrowers per scheme after two years of operation, with wide variation by town size
    32	(Carraway Trust, 2022). The same survey reported a median household saving of GBP 60 a year
    33	among borrowers who answered its questionnaire.
    34	Repeat borrowing, the share of borrowers who borrow more than once, is often used as a sign
    35	that a scheme has become part of household routines. It was 34 percent at the Harwick Tool
    36	Library in its second year (Pemberton and Shah, 2021) and 39 percent at the Otterburn Share
    37	Shed (Lindqvist, 2023). Damage rates reported by tool libraries usually fall between 2 and 5
    38	percent of loans, with power tools at the upper end of that range (Odum, 2020).
    39	Estimates of environmental benefit vary more widely. Faraday and Mbeki (2022) estimated that
    40	a large urban scheme avoided 52 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in a year, but noted
    41	that the result depended heavily on what borrowers said they would otherwise have bought. No
    42	published study that we are aware of has followed a scheme in a town of Brackenford's size
    43	for more than one year.
    44	
    45	3 Methods
    46	3.1 The scheme
    47	At launch the catalogue held 164 items, chosen by library staff after a public consultation,
    48	and by March 2025 it had grown to 236 items. Standard members paid between GBP 1 and GBP 6
    49	per loan, depending on the item, while members receiving Council Tax Reduction borrowed free
    50	of charge. Staff checked each item on return against a written checklist and recorded any
    51	damage on the loan record.
    52	3.2 Membership and loan records
    53	We analysed the anonymised membership and loan records for the whole pilot period. Each loan
    54	record held the item, the branch, the dates of issue and return, the fee paid and any damage
    55	recorded at return. Membership records held the branch of registration and the home
    56	postcode, which we used to assign each borrower to a deprivation quintile of the Index of
    57	Multiple Deprivation.
    58	3.3 Borrower survey
    59	In February 2025 we sent an online survey to all 1,421 members who had borrowed at least one
    60	item, and paper copies were offered at all three branches. The survey asked what borrowers
    61	had used items for, what they would have done without the scheme, and how much they thought
    62	they had saved. It received 426 responses, a response rate of 30 percent.
    63	3.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
    64	We estimated avoided purchases by applying the share of survey respondents who said they
    65	would otherwise have bought each type of item to the number of different members who
    66	borrowed that type of item, so that repeat loans of the same item by the same member were
    67	counted once. Emissions were then estimated from the weight and main material of each type
    68	of item, using published factors for the manufacture of household equipment (Faraday and
    69	Mbeki, 2022).
    70	
    71	3.5 Analysis
    72	We report counts and percentages for the whole pilot and for each year, where year one runs
    73	from April 2023 to March 2024 and year two from April 2024 to March 2025. Before analysis we
    74	removed 203 loan records that staff had created to test the booking system or that had been
    75	recorded twice because of a software fault in the summer of 2023.
    76	4 Results
    77	4.1 Membership and reach
    78	By the end of March 2025, 1,936 people had registered as borrowers across the three
    79	branches. Just over half registered at Central, which is the largest branch and the only one
    80	open on Sundays (Table 1).
    81	Table 1. Registered borrowers by branch of registration, April 2023 to March 2025
    82	Branch Registered borrowers Share of registrations Concession members
    83	Central 1,012 52 percent 198
    84	Eastgate 538 28 percent 171
    85	Millbrook 386 20 percent 94
    86	All branches 1,936 100 percent 463
    87	Of the 1,490 borrowers with a usable home postcode, 611 (41 percent) lived in neighbourhoods
    88	in the two most deprived quintiles. This is close to the 40 percent of Brackenford residents
    89	who live in those neighbourhoods. The remaining 446 registrations had no usable postcode,
    90	mostly because borrowers had registered with a work address, and they are not included in
    91	this figure.
    92	
    93	4.2 Loans and repeat use
    94	Borrowers made 5,712 loans over the two years, 2,214 in year one and 3,498 in year two. This
    95	rise of 58 percent came mostly from Central and Eastgate, where reservations could be
    96	collected on the same day from the spring of 2024. Loans peaked in May and August of each
    97	year and were lowest in January.
    98	Of the 1,936 registered borrowers, 1,421 made at least one loan. Among these active
    99	borrowers, 668 borrowed more than once. That is a repeat borrowing rate of 47 percent, and
   100	it was 53 percent among those who joined in year one and 38 percent among those who joined
   101	in year two, who had less time to borrow again.
   102	The ten most borrowed items accounted for 45 percent of all loans (Table 2). Decorating and
   103	cleaning equipment was borrowed most in spring, and garden and outdoor equipment in summer.
   104	Table 2. The ten most borrowed items, April 2023 to March 2025
   105	Item Loans Share of all loans
   106	Carpet cleaner 418 7.3 percent
   107	Pressure washer 377 6.6 percent
   108	Hedge trimmer 301 5.3 percent
   109	Sewing machine 266 4.7 percent
   110	Wallpaper steamer 244 4.3 percent
   111	Gazebo 231 4.0 percent
   112	Cordless drill 219 3.8 percent
   113	Projector and screen 187 3.3 percent
   114	Four-person tent 171 3.0 percent
   115	Paint sprayer 158 2.8 percent
   116	
   117	4.3 Savings to households
   118	Survey respondents estimated that borrowing instead of buying or hiring had saved their
   119	household a median of GBP 85 over the previous twelve months. Savings were largest among
   120	those who had borrowed decorating equipment, for whom the median was GBP 120. These
   121	estimates are self-reported, and respondents may have overstated what they would otherwise
   122	have spent.
   123	Asked what they would have done without the scheme, 62 percent of respondents said they
   124	would have bought the item, 21 percent would have borrowed it from friends or family, 9
   125	percent would have hired it and 8 percent would have gone without.
   126	4.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
   127	Applying these answers to the 1,820 combinations of member and item type in the loan
   128	records, we estimate that the pilot avoided the purchase of about 1,130 items with a
   129	combined weight of 14.6 tonnes. These avoided purchases correspond to around 38 tonnes of
   130	carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years, mostly from power tools and garden machinery.
   131	The estimate is an upper bound, because it assumes that every respondent who said they would
   132	have bought an item would in fact have done so.
   133	
   134	4.5 Condition of returned items
   135	Staff recorded damage at return on 3.1 percent of loans. A further 19 items were lost or
   136	never returned, equal to 0.3 percent of loans. Repairs and replacements cost GBP 2,460 over
   137	the two years, or about 43 pence per loan. Damage was most common for power tools and garden
   138	equipment (Table 3).
   139	Table 3. Loans with damage recorded at return, by item category
   140	Category Loans Returned damaged Damage rate
   141	Power tools 1,240 64 5.2 percent
   142	Garden equipment 1,105 47 4.3 percent
   143	Cleaning equipment 1,032 29 2.8 percent
   144	Sewing and craft 602 10 1.7 percent
   145	Camping and events 894 19 2.1 percent
   146	Electronics 839 8 1.0 percent
   147	All categories 5,712 177 3.1 percent
   148	5 Discussion
   149	The pilot reached more people than most schemes of its kind, and registrations were well
   150	above the median reported for English schemes after two years. Use also grew steadily
   151	through the second year. Repeat borrowing was higher than in the two schemes reviewed in
   152	Section 2, which suggests that a core group of households has made borrowing a habit.
   153	Borrowers' estimates of what they saved were larger than in the national survey, but they
   154	remain small in relation to household budgets. The scheme's main value to many members may
   155	lie less in money saved than in access to equipment they could not store or could not
   156	justify buying.
   157	
   158	The environmental benefits are real but uncertain. Our estimate of avoided emissions depends
   159	on what borrowers said they would otherwise have done, and on factors for manufacturing
   160	emissions that are themselves approximate.
   161	6 Limitations
   162	The evaluation had no comparison group, so we cannot say how many borrowers would have found
   163	other ways to share or hire equipment. The survey reached only 30 percent of active
   164	borrowers, and those who responded may have been more positive about the scheme than those
   165	who did not. Damage was recorded by staff at the point of return, so faults found later,
   166	when items were next checked or lent, are not counted. The evaluation did not assess effects
   167	on local retailers, such as hardware and DIY shops, or on commercial hire firms.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	The Library of Things pilot met its aims for reach and regular use, and it delivered savings
   170	and environmental benefits that, while uncertain in size, point in the right direction. We
   171	recommend that Brackenford Libraries continue the scheme, record damage throughout an item's
   172	life rather than only at return, and use loan data to guide which items are bought.
   173	
   174	Acknowledgements
   175	We thank the staff of Central, Eastgate and Millbrook libraries, the borrowers who completed
   176	the survey, and the Halden Foundation, which funded both the pilot and this evaluation.
   177	References
   178	Carraway Trust (2022) Libraries of things in England: a survey of 14 schemes. Carraway
   179	Trust.
   180	Faraday, L and Mbeki, T (2022) Counting the carbon in shared equipment. Journal of Circular
   181	Economy Studies, 4(2), 51 to 66.
   182	Lindqvist, A (2023) The Otterburn Share Shed: second-year review. Otterburn Community Trust.
   183	Odum, K (2020) Wear and tear in tool libraries. Community Lending Review, 7, 12 to 19.
   184	Pemberton, J and Shah, R (2021) Who borrows tools? Evidence from the Harwick Tool Library.
   185	Local Economy Notes, 15, 3 to 11.

The Library of Things pilot saved “around 38 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years.”

ANSWER: around 38 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years.

The report estimates that the Library of Things pilot “avoided the purchase of about 1,130 items with a combined weight of 14.6 tonnes” and that these avoided purchases “correspond to around 38 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years.” It also says this is “an upper bound.”

ANSWER: around 38 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years, as an upper-bound estimate.

     1	Borrowing instead of buying: evaluation of the Brackenford Library of Things pilot, April 2023 to March 2025
     2	Northfold Social Research, for Brackenford Libraries. Final report, September 2025.
     3	Abstract
     4	The Brackenford Library of Things lends household tools and equipment from three branch
     5	libraries for a small fee. This report evaluates the first two years of the pilot, from
     6	April 2023 to March 2025, using membership and loan records, a survey of borrowers and the
     7	checks that staff make when items are returned. Almost 2,000 residents registered as
     8	borrowers, and loans grew by 64 percent between the first and second years. Borrowers
     9	reported modest savings, and most items came back in good condition. Registrations from
    10	deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with their share of the town's population. We
    11	recommend that the scheme continues, with changes to how damage is recorded and how new
    12	items are chosen.
    13	1 Introduction
    14	Libraries of things apply the familiar library model to objects that households need only
    15	occasionally, such as drills, gazebos and sewing machines. Their supporters argue that
    16	borrowing saves money, reduces the number of rarely used items that people buy, and brings
    17	people into libraries who would not otherwise visit.
    18	Brackenford Libraries opened its Library of Things in April 2023 with a grant of GBP 96,000
    19	from the Halden Foundation, which also funded this evaluation. The pilot ran from three of
    20	the town's seven branch libraries: Central, Eastgate and Millbrook.
    21	
    22	Items could be reserved online and collected from any of the three branches, and loans
    23	lasted up to seven days. This report sets out what the pilot achieved against the aims
    24	agreed with the funder: to reach a broad range of residents, to build regular use, to save
    25	households money and to reduce waste. Section 2 summarises earlier evaluations of similar
    26	schemes, Section 3 describes our methods, Section 4 presents the results, and Sections 5 to
    27	7 discuss them.
    28	2 Previous studies
    29	Published evaluations of libraries of things are few, and most describe a single scheme in
    30	its first years. A survey of 14 schemes in England found a median of 1,150 registered
    31	borrowers per scheme after two years of operation, with wide variation by town size
    32	(Carraway Trust, 2022). The same survey reported a median household saving of GBP 60 a year
    33	among borrowers who answered its questionnaire.
    34	Repeat borrowing, the share of borrowers who borrow more than once, is often used as a sign
    35	that a scheme has become part of household routines. It was 34 percent at the Harwick Tool
    36	Library in its second year (Pemberton and Shah, 2021) and 39 percent at the Otterburn Share
    37	Shed (Lindqvist, 2023). Damage rates reported by tool libraries usually fall between 2 and 5
    38	percent of loans, with power tools at the upper end of that range (Odum, 2020).
    39	Estimates of environmental benefit vary more widely. Faraday and Mbeki (2022) estimated that
    40	a large urban scheme avoided 52 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in a year, but noted
    41	that the result depended heavily on what borrowers said they would otherwise have bought. No
    42	published study that we are aware of has followed a scheme in a town of Brackenford's size
    43	for more than one year.
    44	
    45	3 Methods
    46	3.1 The scheme
    47	At launch the catalogue held 164 items, chosen by library staff after a public consultation,
    48	and by March 2025 it had grown to 236 items. Standard members paid between GBP 1 and GBP 6
    49	per loan, depending on the item, while members receiving Council Tax Reduction borrowed free
    50	of charge. Staff checked each item on return against a written checklist and recorded any
    51	damage on the loan record.
    52	3.2 Membership and loan records
    53	We analysed the anonymised membership and loan records for the whole pilot period. Each loan
    54	record held the item, the branch, the dates of issue and return, the fee paid and any damage
    55	recorded at return. Membership records held the branch of registration and the home
    56	postcode, which we used to assign each borrower to a deprivation quintile of the Index of
    57	Multiple Deprivation.
    58	3.3 Borrower survey
    59	In February 2025 we sent an online survey to all 1,421 members who had borrowed at least one
    60	item, and paper copies were offered at all three branches. The survey asked what borrowers
    61	had used items for, what they would have done without the scheme, and how much they thought
    62	they had saved. It received 426 responses, a response rate of 30 percent.
    63	3.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
    64	We estimated avoided purchases by applying the share of survey respondents who said they
    65	would otherwise have bought each type of item to the number of different members who
    66	borrowed that type of item, so that repeat loans of the same item by the same member were
    67	counted once. Emissions were then estimated from the weight and main material of each type
    68	of item, using published factors for the manufacture of household equipment (Faraday and
    69	Mbeki, 2022).
    70	
    71	3.5 Analysis
    72	We report counts and percentages for the whole pilot and for each year, where year one runs
    73	from April 2023 to March 2024 and year two from April 2024 to March 2025. Before analysis we
    74	removed 203 loan records that staff had created to test the booking system or that had been
    75	recorded twice because of a software fault in the summer of 2023.
    76	4 Results
    77	4.1 Membership and reach
    78	By the end of March 2025, 1,936 people had registered as borrowers across the three
    79	branches. Just over half registered at Central, which is the largest branch and the only one
    80	open on Sundays (Table 1).
    81	Table 1. Registered borrowers by branch of registration, April 2023 to March 2025
    82	Branch Registered borrowers Share of registrations Concession members
    83	Central 1,012 52 percent 198
    84	Eastgate 538 28 percent 171
    85	Millbrook 386 20 percent 94
    86	All branches 1,936 100 percent 463
    87	Of the 1,490 borrowers with a usable home postcode, 611 (41 percent) lived in neighbourhoods
    88	in the two most deprived quintiles. This is close to the 40 percent of Brackenford residents
    89	who live in those neighbourhoods. The remaining 446 registrations had no usable postcode,
    90	mostly because borrowers had registered with a work address, and they are not included in
    91	this figure.
    92	
    93	4.2 Loans and repeat use
    94	Borrowers made 5,712 loans over the two years, 2,214 in year one and 3,498 in year two. This
    95	rise of 58 percent came mostly from Central and Eastgate, where reservations could be
    96	collected on the same day from the spring of 2024. Loans peaked in May and August of each
    97	year and were lowest in January.
    98	Of the 1,936 registered borrowers, 1,421 made at least one loan. Among these active
    99	borrowers, 668 borrowed more than once. That is a repeat borrowing rate of 47 percent, and
   100	it was 53 percent among those who joined in year one and 38 percent among those who joined
   101	in year two, who had less time to borrow again.
   102	The ten most borrowed items accounted for 45 percent of all loans (Table 2). Decorating and
   103	cleaning equipment was borrowed most in spring, and garden and outdoor equipment in summer.
   104	Table 2. The ten most borrowed items, April 2023 to March 2025
   105	Item Loans Share of all loans
   106	Carpet cleaner 418 7.3 percent
   107	Pressure washer 377 6.6 percent
   108	Hedge trimmer 301 5.3 percent
   109	Sewing machine 266 4.7 percent
   110	Wallpaper steamer 244 4.3 percent
   111	Gazebo 231 4.0 percent
   112	Cordless drill 219 3.8 percent
   113	Projector and screen 187 3.3 percent
   114	Four-person tent 171 3.0 percent
   115	Paint sprayer 158 2.8 percent
   116	
   117	4.3 Savings to households
   118	Survey respondents estimated that borrowing instead of buying or hiring had saved their
   119	household a median of GBP 85 over the previous twelve months. Savings were largest among
   120	those who had borrowed decorating equipment, for whom the median was GBP 120. These
   121	estimates are self-reported, and respondents may have overstated what they would otherwise
   122	have spent.
   123	Asked what they would have done without the scheme, 62 percent of respondents said they
   124	would have bought the item, 21 percent would have borrowed it from friends or family, 9
   125	percent would have hired it and 8 percent would have gone without.
   126	4.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
   127	Applying these answers to the 1,820 combinations of member and item type in the loan
   128	records, we estimate that the pilot avoided the purchase of about 1,130 items with a
   129	combined weight of 14.6 tonnes. These avoided purchases correspond to around 38 tonnes of
   130	carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years, mostly from power tools and garden machinery.
   131	The estimate is an upper bound, because it assumes that every respondent who said they would
   132	have bought an item would in fact have done so.
   133	
   134	4.5 Condition of returned items
   135	Staff recorded damage at return on 3.1 percent of loans. A further 19 items were lost or
   136	never returned, equal to 0.3 percent of loans. Repairs and replacements cost GBP 2,460 over
   137	the two years, or about 43 pence per loan. Damage was most common for power tools and garden
   138	equipment (Table 3).
   139	Table 3. Loans with damage recorded at return, by item category
   140	Category Loans Returned damaged Damage rate
   141	Power tools 1,240 64 5.2 percent
   142	Garden equipment 1,105 47 4.3 percent
   143	Cleaning equipment 1,032 29 2.8 percent
   144	Sewing and craft 602 10 1.7 percent
   145	Camping and events 894 19 2.1 percent
   146	Electronics 839 8 1.0 percent
   147	All categories 5,712 177 3.1 percent
   148	5 Discussion
   149	The pilot reached more people than most schemes of its kind, and registrations were well
   150	above the median reported for English schemes after two years. Use also grew steadily
   151	through the second year. Repeat borrowing was higher than in the two schemes reviewed in
   152	Section 2, which suggests that a core group of households has made borrowing a habit.
   153	Borrowers' estimates of what they saved were larger than in the national survey, but they
   154	remain small in relation to household budgets. The scheme's main value to many members may
   155	lie less in money saved than in access to equipment they could not store or could not
   156	justify buying.
   157	
   158	The environmental benefits are real but uncertain. Our estimate of avoided emissions depends
   159	on what borrowers said they would otherwise have done, and on factors for manufacturing
   160	emissions that are themselves approximate.
   161	6 Limitations
   162	The evaluation had no comparison group, so we cannot say how many borrowers would have found
   163	other ways to share or hire equipment. The survey reached only 30 percent of active
   164	borrowers, and those who responded may have been more positive about the scheme than those
   165	who did not. Damage was recorded by staff at the point of return, so faults found later,
   166	when items were next checked or lent, are not counted. The evaluation did not assess effects
   167	on local retailers, such as hardware and DIY shops, or on commercial hire firms.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	The Library of Things pilot met its aims for reach and regular use, and it delivered savings
   170	and environmental benefits that, while uncertain in size, point in the right direction. We
   171	recommend that Brackenford Libraries continue the scheme, record damage throughout an item's
   172	life rather than only at return, and use loan data to guide which items are bought.
   173	
   174	Acknowledgements
   175	We thank the staff of Central, Eastgate and Millbrook libraries, the borrowers who completed
   176	the survey, and the Halden Foundation, which funded both the pilot and this evaluation.
   177	References
   178	Carraway Trust (2022) Libraries of things in England: a survey of 14 schemes. Carraway
   179	Trust.
   180	Faraday, L and Mbeki, T (2022) Counting the carbon in shared equipment. Journal of Circular
   181	Economy Studies, 4(2), 51 to 66.
   182	Lindqvist, A (2023) The Otterburn Share Shed: second-year review. Otterburn Community Trust.
   183	Odum, K (2020) Wear and tear in tool libraries. Community Lending Review, 7, 12 to 19.
   184	Pemberton, J and Shah, R (2021) Who borrows tools? Evidence from the Harwick Tool Library.
   185	Local Economy Notes, 15, 3 to 11.

Reviews/Heat pump programme board notes.md:3:## Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024
     1	# Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024
     2	
     3	## Kestle Bay heat pump programme: board meeting notes, 14 November 2024
     4	
     5	Present: Rosa Penhallow (chair), Daniel Kitto, Meera Joshi, Tom Rowe and Ellen Vosper (programme manager). Apologies: Gareth Lobb.
     6	
     7	## Progress
     8	
     9	Ellen reported that the first phase closed in September with 214 installations. Installers now report a median of 9 weeks between the home survey and the installation date, down from 14 weeks in the first year of the programme.
    10	
    11	## Installers
    12	
    13	Brightwater Heating withdrew from the programme in August because of staff shortages, leaving Pellow and Sons as the only appointed installer. The board agreed to run a new tender in January to appoint at least one more installer before phase two begins.
    14	
    15	## Complaints
    16	
    17	Six formal complaints were received in 2024, four of them about installation delays and two about the condition of gardens after outdoor units were fitted. All have been resolved.
    18	
    19	## Phase two
    20	
    21	The board agreed a target of 150 further installations by March 2026, with priority for homes heated by oil or bottled gas. It also agreed to cap the householder contribution at GBP 4,000 for households receiving means-tested benefits, with the society's hardship fund meeting the rest of the cost.
    22	
    23	## Actions
    24	
    25	Ellen to draft the installer tender by 12 December. Daniel to ask the Coastal Communities Net Zero Fund whether the grant can stay at GBP 6,000 per home in phase two. Meera to update the website with the new waiting times.
